ENTERIC FEVER LESIONS IN DOGS. 
A Contribution towards the Investigation of the Prevalence of 
Enteric Fever in Cantonments. 
By J. R. ROBERTS, M.B., M.S., F.R.C.S., Eng., 
Indian Medical Service. 
This article is written with a view to point 
out a direction in which farther investigation 
might be made, in order to attempt the solution 
of the question of the continued prevalence 
of Enteric fever in cantonments. 
The work 
begun has, through the devolving of certain 
duties on the writer, been left unfinished ; he 
is anxious, however, that those whose oppor- 
tunities admit of it, do push the enquiry towards 
final solution. 
Stationed at Sialkot during the past cold 
weather, it was noticed that there was a heavy 
mortality among dogs of European breeds ; 
that lung and bowel complaints prevailed, with 
here and there a case of rabies. A series of post- 
mortem examinations on healthy dogs and dogs 
dying of disease were begun, resulting in the 
fiuding of Enteric fever lesions in the intestiues,

The peculiarity of this case is, that lesions 
were found in the large intestine resembling 
dysentery, though by no means so intense ; a pre- 
vious post-mortem on a dog suffering from 
abdominal pain and p tssiitg blood-stained stools, 
shews a condition to which no oilier name but 
dysentery could be given, viz., intense conges- 
tion of miiC'ius membrane with submucous 
haemorrhages, most, marked towards the rectum ; 
but in this case there were no lesions of the 
small intestine whatsoever. 
The condition of the 
vermiform appendix, though, this organ is> small 
in carnivorn, but communicates freely with the 
coecum, need be no mutter of surprise, tor its 
mucous membrane being composed principally 
of solitary glands, can well be associated with 
other enteric phenomena. 
This is seen in the 
human being, as in a recent case at Sialkot (A. 
death 28th April 1889,) where the appendix 
was very much inflamed. 
The varying of Indian typhoid from the 
European type is a phenomena noticed by alt. 
That this is dependent on some relation to malaria, 
or to the position and extent of the lesions, 
and the liability of other parts of the intestines 
to be attacked in India, as well as those more 
commonly affected in Europe, still remains, I 
imagine:, sub judice. 
A series of cases such as 
occurred at the Station Hospital, Sialkot, and 
in which, besides ulcers more or less healed 
in the ileum, there was found extensive ulcera- 
tion of the large intestine, is> no doubt,, a com- 
mon enough experience of post-mortems on 
enteric eases in India. 
Evidence as to lesions 
occurring higher up mighty I have no doubt,, be 
collected,, as shewn in a case (Private J. B., 
death 6th March 1889-, at Sialkot), when on 
examination of the intestines from below up- 
wards, ulcers of Peyer's patches were succeeded 
by small superficial ragged ulcers extending into 
the upper portion of the jejunum. 
It will be 
interesting to note how far the analogy of

To prove that dogs area con-

in Indian cantonments, in spite of sanitation,

Yet cannot dog's ejecta, scattered as it, is about 
compounds, near wells, in barracks and even 
bungalows, be a fertile enough source of enteric 
fever?dogs as we know entering so much into 
the Indian life of private soldier, officer and 
civilian alike. 
Lastly, I would point out to those commenc- 
ing post-mortems on dogs that the lower part 
of the ileum mucous membrane is naturally 
honey-combed in appearance, tlnitPcyer'spatches 
are well marked and raised above the surface,

Besides these they will 
find a wealth of malarious spleens, of submu-

acute disease, such as pneumonia, and at another, 
disappointing though it may seem, no naked eye
